title: The Only Free Lunch in Investing
subtitle: Yesterday: no reward without risk. Today: the one trick that lets you cut risk without cutting expected return. Economists literally call it the only free lunch.
hook: We just said there's no free lunch — higher return demands higher risk. There's exactly *one* loophole, and it's so good economists named it 'the only free lunch in finance': **diversification.** Spread your money across things that don't move in lockstep and you can shrink the bumps *without* giving up expected return. Here's why that's almost magic.

sections.heading: Why one basket is dangerous
sections.body: Put everything in a single stock and your fate is welded to that one company. It could soar — or a scandal, a bad quarter, or a fire could wipe you out. That's **specific risk**: danger unique to one holding, and it's the kind you're *not* rewarded for taking, because you could have avoided it for free.

sections.heading: How spreading out cancels the noise
sections.body: Hold 30 different companies across industries and something wonderful happens: their individual ups and downs partly **cancel out**. One firm's disaster is another's windfall; the random, company-specific noise averages toward zero, while the broad market's return stays. You keep the reward and shed the avoidable risk — as long as your holdings don't all rise and fall *together* (low **correlation** is the key).

sections.caption: Add more uncorrelated holdings and the jagged, company-specific risk falls away — leaving the market risk you're actually paid to bear.

sections.label: The catch: correlation
sections.body: Diversification only works if your holdings don't move together. Ten tech stocks aren't diversified — they crash as one. True diversification mixes things that respond differently to the world (stocks vs. bonds, different regions/sectors). And in a real panic, correlations spike (everything falls together), which is diversification's great disappointment — it helps most of the time, least when you most want it.

sections.caption: Diversification in plain terms — why not to put all your eggs in one basket.

takeaways: **Diversification** is 'the only free lunch': less risk *without* less expected return.
**Specific risk** (one company's fate) is avoidable — so you're not rewarded for it.
Holding many **uncorrelated** things lets company-specific noise cancel out.
You're left with **market risk** — the kind you actually get paid to bear.
It fails when correlations spike (panics) — everything can fall together.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: Yesterday said you're paid for risk. So why isn't specific (single-company) risk rewarded?
options: Because you could eliminate it for free by diversifying — markets don't pay you to take avoidable risk
quiz.explain: You're only compensated for risk you can't diversify away (market risk). Avoidable risk earns no premium.

tg_quiz.correct: Right — diversification needs things that don't move together.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's the mixed one — 10 tech stocks all crash together.
tg_quiz.explain: Low correlation is what makes the noise cancel.
